History:
- Presenting complaint: Shortness of breath and localized rash after suspected wasp/bee sting to arm.
- Onset/duration: “A few minutes ago” prior to consult.
- Progression: Patient anxious; reports slight right-sided lip sensation/swelling and “tongue feels weird.” Breathing feels not “particularly acute” at time of call.
- Site/skin findings: Arm sting site with slight redness, puncture mark, blotchy rash; no notable swelling per patient.
- Triggers/context: Outdoor exposure; insect identified as bee or wasp (unsure).
- Associated symptoms: Anxiety. Denies prior anaphylaxis. No current stridor reported.
- Previous episodes: None reported. No prior EpiPen.

Past Medical History:
- Conditions: Eczema (past).
- Allergies: Penicillin (reaction not specified). No known food or pet allergies.
- Medications: None reported; not on anxiety medication; no EpiPen.
- Hospitalizations/surgeries: Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- General: Speaking in full sentences; no distress observed via video.
- Airway/breathing: No visible lip swelling on video; oropharyngeal view appeared normal; no visible throat swelling; no audible stridor; breathing appeared normal to clinician.
- Skin (arm): Localized erythema with puncture mark; blotchy rash; no obvious swelling noted on video or by patient.
- Neurologic/mental status: Alert; anxious but coherent.

Impression:
- Localized allergic reaction to an insect sting (bee/wasp) without current features of anaphylaxis; health anxiety present.

Management Plan:
- Medications:
  - Chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg up to six times daily; route not documented.
  - Alternative option: once-daily antihistamine (name and dose not documented; route not documented).
- Safety-net/urgent care advice:
  - Seek immediate emergency care (A&E) if any breathing difficulty, swelling of lips/tongue, voice change, stridor, or rapid progression of symptoms.
  - If local redness spreads, becomes hot/tender, or systemic signs develop, contact clinic; may need antibiotic evaluation for possible local infection.
- Education:
  - Provided information link on signs/symptoms of anaphylaxis.
  - Reassurance that current presentation suggests localized reaction; most severe reactions occur immediately.
- Follow-up:
  - Return to clinic if symptoms worsen, do not improve, or if recurrent similar reactions occur.
  - Consider allergy evaluation if reactions become recurrent or non-specific rashes persist.

Patient Summary:
- Adult male developed a localized erythematous rash with puncture mark on the arm minutes after a bee/wasp sting, with anxiety and subjective mild lip/tongue sensations but no objective airway compromise on video exam.
- Clinical picture consistent with localized allergic reaction; no current evidence of anaphylaxis.
- Plan: Start antihistamine, monitor closely, emergency precautions reviewed, and follow-up as needed.

Key Takeaways:
- Start an antihistamine as advised and monitor the sting site.
- Go to A&E immediately for breathing difficulty, lip/tongue swelling, or stridor.
- Seek care if redness spreads or becomes hot/painful, suggesting possible infection.

Next Steps:
- Begin OTC antihistamine today.
- Self-monitor for 24–48 hours; contact clinic if worsening or persistent symptoms.
- If episodes recur, discuss need for further evaluation (e.g., allergy assessment).

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vital signs; complete medication list and doses; past surgical/hospitalization history; smoking/alcohol history; tetanus immunization status; specific penicillin reaction details; detailed respiratory exam (in-person) and peak flow/oxygen saturation.
- Internal conflicts: Patient stated age “27 years,” but gave DOB as 11/17/1991 (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: Minor transcription artifacts and filler; clinical content sufficient for a telehealth assessment.
